works.title: The Crucifixion of Saint Andrew
works.alt: Caravaggio painting: an old man bound to a cross in deep shadow, an executioner on a ladder reaching up toward the ropes with his arms raised, onlookers below lit from the left.
works.label: Painted in Naples, in the months after Caravaggio fled Rome under sentence of death for killing a man. The legend holds that Andrew preached from the cross for two days until the crowd demanded his release, and that the executioner sent to cut him down found his hands would not move. That is the instant here: the man on the ladder, arms up, stopped.

works.title: Island of the Dead
works.alt: Böcklin painting: a small rowing boat carrying a white shrouded figure and a draped coffin approaches a rocky island walled with stone, a grove of black cypresses rising at its center.
works.label: The island exists nowhere. A young widow commissioned the picture as a memorial to her husband, and the draped coffin and the white standing figure were added at her request. Cliffs and cypresses drop to near-silhouette, so the only truly lit thing in the painting is the small boat. This is the first of five versions Böcklin painted; the one usually reproduced online is the 1883 Berlin picture.

works.title: The Beacons of Gondor
works.label: Nearly ten feet across, painted in traditional oils from posed models rather than digitally. The beacon fire is the only warm light in the picture, so the whole composition is built out of how far that light carries before it gives out.

works.title: The Harvesters
works.alt: Bruegel painting: a golden wheat field in late summer, peasants cutting a path through the standing corn while others eat and one sleeps beneath a pear tree, a village and bay beyond.
works.label: One of six panels Bruegel painted for a wealthy Antwerp merchant, marking the turns of the year; five survive. It is among the earliest European paintings to treat ordinary labor as a subject worth the whole canvas rather than a detail at the edge of a religious scene. The wheat is waist-high and the cut path through it leads the eye straight back to the village.

works.title: Hen and Rooster with Grapevine
works.medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk, image 101.9 × 41.3 cm
works.alt: Jakuchū hanging scroll: a rooster with a long arching tail and a hen beneath a grapevine heavy with fruit, painted in ink and color on silk.
works.label: Jakuchū ran his family's Kyoto greengrocery for forty years before handing it over to paint full time, and he was seventy-six when he made this. The bird is assembled from hundreds of separate feather strokes rather than massed shapes, and its tail is drawn crossing in front of the grapevine instead of disappearing behind it.

works.title: Ghosts of the Taira at Daimotsu Bay
works.medium: Triptych of woodblock prints (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
works.alt: Kuniyoshi woodblock triptych: a sailing ship crowded with armored warriors rides a towering blue wave, while the ghosts of drowned Taira soldiers rise out of the sea around it.
works.label: Yoshitsune's ship driven into Daimotsu Bay by a storm and set upon by the ghosts of the Taira warriors drowned at Dan-no-ura — the clan his own campaign destroyed. Kuniyoshi returned to the subject more than once. It is a triptych: three separate sheets, designed to hang together so the wave runs unbroken across all three.

works.title: Twilight in the Wilderness
works.alt: Church painting: a wilderness sky at sunset burning orange and crimson in long streaked clouds, above dark silent hills, a river and a line of firs with no people anywhere in it.
works.label: Painted the year before the Civil War began, from studies Church made in Maine, and emptied of every human figure — no cabin, no boat, no road. Almost half the canvas is sky. The red is laid in thin glazes over a pale ground so the clouds appear lit from behind rather than colored on the surface.

works.title: Madame X (Virginie Amélie Avegno Gautreau)
works.alt: Sargent portrait: a woman in a black full-length gown with jeweled straps stands in profile against a dark brown ground, one hand resting on a small table, her skin painted pale lavender-gray.
works.label: The 1884 Paris Salon received it so badly that Sargent left for London and stayed. Gautreau powdered her skin with lavender, and Sargent matched it exactly, which is why she reads almost gray against the black dress and brown ground. The right strap originally hung off her shoulder; he repainted it upright after the Salon, and the picture stayed in his studio for thirty years.

works.title: The Crucifixion
works.medium: Tempera on wood, gold ground, 63.8 × 48.3 cm
works.alt: Fra Angelico panel: Christ on the cross against a flat gold ground, small blue-winged angels in the gold around him, a crowd of soldiers in red caps and riders on horseback below, and the Virgin collapsing in blue while the Marys kneel in pink at the foot of the cross.
works.label: An early panel, small enough that the Metropolitan takes it to have been made for private devotion rather than for an altar. Mourners, soldiers and mounted riders close in a ring around the foot of the cross, a circular arrangement the museum traces to Lorenzo Ghiberti's bronze doors for the Florence Baptistery. Behind the cross there is no sky at all, only gold.

works.title: Icon of the Mother of God and Infant Christ (Virgin Eleousa)
works.medium: Tempera and gold on wood, 96 × 70 cm
works.alt: Cretan icon: the Virgin in a deep red mantle presses her cheek against the infant Christ, who wears a pale blue tunic under a gold-orange wrap and holds a scroll, both set against a worn gold ground.
works.label: Painted on Crete while the island was under Venetian rule, and large enough to have stood on an iconostasis, the screen that closes off the sanctuary in a Greek Orthodox church. The Eleousa, or tenderness, type puts mother and child cheek to cheek rather than facing the congregation straight on. Cleveland gives the panel to Angelos Akotantos, the most sought-after painter in Candia, as an attribution rather than a signature.

works.title: Oedipus and the Sphinx
works.alt: Moreau painting: a sphinx with a woman's head, a lion's body and blue and white wings clings by her claws to the chest of a standing nude Oedipus, the two locked eye to eye on a narrow rock ledge, with a dead man's foot and hand showing at the lower edge.
works.label: Moreau made his name with this picture at the Paris Salon of 1864, at a moment when French painting was turning toward scenes of ordinary modern life. He went the other way, into myth, and a younger generation that included Odilon Redon and Oscar Wilde followed him there. The sphinx has jumped and is holding on by her claws: the riddle is being put at close range, and what is left of the travelers who answered wrong lies on the ledge below.

works.title: The Books of Earthsea: The Complete Illustrated Edition
works.medium: More than fifty color and black-and-white illustrations
works.label: Four years of work, made in close collaboration with Ursula K. Le Guin, who chose the scenes herself and died months before the book appeared. The dragon alone took about a year of revision, each sketch pulling it further from a reptile and closer to a face. Vess keeps the figures small inside large landscapes, so it is the islands rather than the wizards that carry the pictures.

works.title: Blind Orion Searching for the Rising Sun
works.alt: Poussin landscape: the giant Orion strides through a wooded valley with one arm outstretched, a small man riding on his shoulders to point the way and another small figure watching from below, while a woman stands on a dark cloud above him.
works.label: Orion, blinded, walking east toward the sunrise that is to give him back his sight, with Cedalion riding his shoulders to steer him and Hephaestus watching from below. Diana stands on the storm cloud that hangs across his eyes; one long-standing reading takes her presence as notice of the death she will later deal him. Poussin painted it in Rome in 1658 for Michel Passart, a Paris finance official who owned at least seven of his pictures.

works.title: Nur Jahan holding a portrait of Emperor Jahangir
works.medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper; painting 13.6 × 6.4 cm, page 30 × 22.1 cm
works.alt: Mughal album page: a woman in a white striped skirt and orange veil stands barefoot in profile on a plain green ground, holding up a small framed portrait of the bearded emperor, the whole page set in a wide border of white blossoms on dark blue.
works.label: Nur Jahan was the emperor Jahangir's favorite wife and ran much of the business of the state in his name. She holds his portrait here after his death, shown in an idealized youth — she was about fifty when he died — while he appears aged behind the rail that marked imperial presence. The painting itself is only about five inches tall; everything outside that narrow panel is the album border.

works.title: Streams and Mountains
works.medium: Hanging scroll; ink on paper, image 92.2 × 37.6 cm
works.alt: Chinese hanging scroll in ink: a mountain mass built from dense fine strokes rises the full height of the sheet, trees and a thatched retreat beside a stream at the bottom, columns of inscription across the top and red collectors' seals at the edges.
works.label: Painted during one of the stretches Xu Ben spent in retreat from official life, in the years when the Yuan dynasty was giving way to the Ming. The mountain is built almost entirely from repeated hemp-fiber strokes, so the rock reads as one continuous rhythm rather than as separate masses stacked up. At the base, a scholar comes up through the trees on foot toward the hermit's house.

works.title: Wheat Fields
works.alt: Ruisdael landscape: a broad sandy track runs between pale ripening wheat fields toward a stand of trees and a few low roofs, two small figures walking on the path, with a tall bank of cumulus filling more than half the sky.
works.label: More than half the canvas is given to the clouds, and the land below is arranged to serve them: the track widens as it comes forward, and the two figures on it are small enough to set the scale of everything else. The wheat is pale and nearly ready to cut. Ruisdael and his generation worked the horizon this low so that weather could be the real subject of a landscape.

works.title: The Birth of Venus
works.alt: Cabanel painting: a nude Venus lies stretched full length along the crest of a green wave, her long auburn hair trailing in the water and one arm raised across her eyes, while a flight of winged cherubs crosses the pale sky above her, two of them blowing conch shells.
works.label: This is the Metropolitan's picture, painted in 1875 for the New York collector John Wolfe; the first and slightly larger version made a sensation at the Salon of 1863, was bought by Napoleon III, and is now in the Musée d'Orsay. Cabanel finishes the sea as smoothly as the figure and leaves no visible brushwork anywhere, which is precisely what the next generation of French painters would attack. Venus does not stand on a shell here but lies along the wave, arm across her face, somewhere between waking and not.

works.title: Young Woman Knitting
works.alt: Morisot painting: a young woman in a straw hat and pale jacket sits knitting on a slatted garden chair beside a flowering border, a second empty chair standing on the gravel path at the right, the whole picture brushed in loose strokes of green, cream and pink.
works.label: Morisot was a founding member of the Impressionist group and showed in all but one of its eight exhibitions. The paint is left open here — the gravel path and the empty chair are barely more than dragged strokes over the ground — and the hands, the one part of the picture actually doing work, are the least finished thing in it. Her signature sits at the lower left in the same thin paint as the garden.
